method: Direct retrieval of public scholarly/institutional sources; PDFs downloaded to reports/supplement-opencode-1/scratch/source-recheck-africa/ and converted with pdftotext -layout so excerpts come from retrieved full text, not search snippets. Printed-page locators verified against page headers/footers inside the retrieved PDFs.

audits.claim: Raia's colophon discussion distinguishes copyist and owner from author; their names cannot be collapsed into a single 'creator' field.
audits.retrieval_status: retrieved: full article PDF (25 pp.), text layer extracted; printed pp. 69–70 located
audits.source_locator: printed p. 69: colophon transcription/translation of 'Utenzi wa Yaaqubu, manuscript 352' and Fig. 1 caption; printed p. 70: discussion of the two names
audits.source_excerpt: The two names mentioned in this colophon have two different roles ascribed to them: while the first one ... was the person in charge of copying the manuscript ... Shehe Hamadi wa Shehe Pate was the manuscript's owner.
audits.basis: PASSAGE RETRIEVED. The same retrieved text continues: 'Thus, the author is not mentioned, whereas the scribe and the owner of the copy are.' (p. 70). Page attribution checked against the running head + page number ('RAIA | TRANSMISSION AND TEXTUAL VARIANTS 69' and '70 ...') inside the same PDF text.
audits.access_limit: Text layer only; manuscript page images/figures not visually inspected.

audits.claim: KTD-S-0006 and §2 cite [RAI] as 'Printed pp. 65–71', which can be read as the article's printed extent.
audits.retrieval_status: retrieved: full issue article list plus full article text; final article page located
audits.source_locator: issue article list (p. 65 entry for Raia; p. 87 entry for Vierke); running heads/page numbers 72, 74, 76, 78, 80, 82, 84, 86 on Raia's article pages; end matter on printed p. 86
audits.source_excerpt: 65 | A Network of Copies: Transmission and Textual Variants of Manuscript Traditions from the J. W. T. Allen Collection (Dar es Salaam) Annachiara Raia / 87 | Writing Songs, Singing Texts: Orality and Literacy in Swahili Manuscripts Clarissa Vierke
audits.basis: The article's printed extent is pp. 65–86, not pp. 65–71. The inspected sub-range stated in the entry is not false as a reading record (collection history, copying network, and the p. 69–70 colophon discussion sit inside it), but the citation understates the source and the KTD-S-0006 phrase 'variant groups' points past p. 71: the Group I–III variant sections, Tables 2–3, and the orthographic-variant discussion continue on pp. 72–86. Dated erratum appended to the entry.
audits.access_limit: Text layer only; reproduced manuscript images/figures not visually inspected.

audits.claim: The 2011 Songo Mnara report records a coin-and-carnelian deposit beneath the floor of SM017 and shell objects in SM023, then suggests structured deposition connected with houses [SM11, 'House Excavations,' p. 6].
audits.retrieval_status: retrieved: full field-report PDF (6 pp.), text extracted; page footers read as printed pp. 3–8
audits.source_excerpt: A hoard of 360 Kilwa-type coins was found beneath the floor of SM017, accompanied by a carnelian necklace. SM023 contained instead a small pit into which eight large aragonite (clam shell) beads or spindle whorls had been placed.
audits.basis: PASSAGE RETRIEVED at the cited page (p. 6 confirmed by the page-number footer sequence 3–8 across the PDF's six pages). The interpretive sentence follows immediately: 'These comparable but different deposits suggest deliberate acts of structured deposition that might be linked to the meanings and value of the houses'. The entry keeps observation and interpretation separate, matching the source's own 'suggest ... might be' hedging.
audits.access_limit: Figures/site plan not inspected; separate specialist analyses (coins, beads, botanical, faunal) reported as pending in the same report.

audits.claim: The Songo Mnara report uses geophysical and artifact-distribution evidence to investigate earthen buildings and open-space activity as well as stonehouses [SM11, 'Geophysical Survey'; 'Open Spaces'] — an era/material coupling, not a bibliography fact.
audits.source_locator: printed pp. 3 and 5, section headings 'Geophysical Survey' and 'Open Spaces'
audits.source_excerpt: magnetometry has illustrated a pattern of anomalous areas that seem to be linked to wattle and daub architecture and associated areas of domestic refuse
audits.basis: Both cited section headings exist. Wattle-and-daub = the entry's 'earthen buildings'; the same sections report shovel tests, soil chemistry, phytoliths, and artifact mapping in open areas, and describe kilwa-type coins/carnelian as 'below-floor' deposits rather than floor assemblages (distinguishing deposition phase from use phase, which is the entry's point). Deposits are dated by the report to the 14th–16th centuries, matching the entry's call to keep calibrated estimates, phase, and period labels distinct.
audits.access_limit: No independent chronometric recalibration attempted; figures not inspected.

audits.claim: The Sanye (ELAR 0836) description discusses a naming preference differing from its catalogue heading ('Dahalo'), reports Swahili explanations alongside Sanye speech, partial annotation, and bundle-level restrictions.
audits.source_locator: collection page fields and 'Sociolinguistic Context → Identity and ethnonyms'; 'Summary of the collection'; 'Collection access and citation'
audits.source_excerpt: The members prefer the self-designation 'Sanye' ... They reject the exonym 'Dahalo' associated with historical stigmatization and mostly common in academia.
audits.basis: PASSAGE RETRIEVED; the page's Language field reads 'Dahalo' while the description states the preference for 'Sanye' ('Wasanye' for people, 'Kisanye' for the language in Swahili), so the entry's separate-fields rule is grounded. The page also states 'many recordings include spontaneous Swahili explanations by Sanye speakers themselves', 'Partial transcriptions and translations (Swahili and English, in progress)', and 'Access restrictions apply as specified in individual bundle metadata' — matching the entry's genre, annotation, and restriction claims. The entry's self-reported limit ('recordings and lexical database not inspected') was respected; the description does not license any lexical extraction.
audits.access_limit: Recordings, photographs, and the FLEx database not accessed; only the public description is quoted.

audits.claim: The Verba Africana descriptions explicitly label several ngoma recordings as planned performances rather than recordings during their associated rituals [VA, items 6–9]; item 3 is tied to the Kéla version.
audits.entry_locator: §4 table row [VA, item 3] (line 70) and bullet (line 74); KTD-S-0008 (line 11)
audits.retrieval_status: retrieved: full World Oral Literature Project collection page (16 items)
audits.source_locator: item descriptions 6–9 ('Ndege we', 'Kyaso', 'Kunguiya and Kilua', 'Chikocha') and item 3 ('Épopée de Soundjata (Sunjata Epic)')
audits.source_excerpt: All the ngoma performances reproduced here are 'planned performances' which means that they were not recorded during the rituals to which they belong.
audits.basis: PASSAGE RETRIEVED and repeated verbatim under items 6, 7, 8, and 9. Item 3 states the two themes 'typical of the version of Kéla', supporting the entry's version-third-party separation; items 4–5 are taarab, 10–12 Ewe migration material, 13–16 Karamojong, matching the entry's 'items 4–16' characterization.
audits.access_limit: Videos not played (page text only), consistent with the entry's stated boundary; performance-internal details therefore remain unverified.

audits.claim: Ostashewski describes the Cape Breton Sunjata production as deliberately concise and explains that Keita's spoken contribution is poetic rendering/paraphrase rather than direct translation [SING]; the credited participants are Hawa Kassé Mady Diabaté (voice), Lassana Diabaté (balafon), Chérif Keita (poetic rendering), Lucy Duran (production).
audits.retrieval_status: retrieved: full article text; issue metadata retrieved from the journal archive
audits.source_locator: sections 'Sung storytelling' and 'Poetic translation and paraphrase'; Figure 1 caption; journal archive listing 'The Sunjata Project in Unama'ki (Cape Breton)… Vol. 14 No. 1 (2025)'
audits.source_excerpt: Rather than offering direct translations, his dramatically-presented texts reflected similar content and carried a narrative that paralleled Hawa's sung story.
audits.basis: PASSAGE RETRIEVED. 'In our concise, theatrical Cape Breton performance of the Sunjata epic' supports the entry's 'deliberately concise' wording; the Figure 1 caption credits 'Lassana Diabaté (balafon), Hawa Kassé Mady Diabaté (vocals), and poetic translation performance by Chérif Keita', and the article names 'director Lucy Duran of ... SOAS'. The 2025 date in KTD-S-0009 is corroborated by the issue record (Vol. 14 No. 1, 2025). Minor note, no erratum: the article's own text spells 'Lucy Duran' without the accent the entry uses once in §4.
audits.access_limit: Films not viewed; the appendix transcript of the performance was not separately examined here.

audits.claim: EAP334/1 Wolofal manuscript: catalogued as likely written in the 1980s from its contents; incomplete and damaged; the entry treats the date as an inference, not a directly dated witness.
audits.retrieval_status: retrieved: British Library catalogue description text
audits.source_locator: collection description for EAP334/1 (physical characteristics and date statement)
audits.source_excerpt: Based upon the events described in the material, it has been written in the 1980's. ... The document is in poor condition. Some pages are lost. The remaining ones have some stains and tears.
audits.basis: PASSAGE RETRIEVED; the record also hedges independently ('Based on the events discussed in the material, it is likely written in the 1980s'), which supports the entry's insistence that an inferred content-based date remains an inference. Record identifies the script as 'Wolof Ajami (Wolofal)' and an 8-page unbound paper manuscript, consistent with the entry's script/genre fields.
audits.access_limit: Manuscript images not examined; the '1980s' inference cannot be tested against the contents from the catalogue alone.

audits.claim: EAP1042/32/5 is a bilingual Arabic–Mandinka Ajami item whose catalogue explicitly requires dual literacy, with genres including correspondence, notes, poem, and divination material; water damage and ink staining are recorded.
audits.source_locator: item 32/5 description fields and physical-characteristics field
audits.source_excerpt: Dual literacy in Arabic and Ajami is needed to fully understand the contents of these materials. ... Some manuscripts are damaged by water. Due to ink stains and water damage, some of the text may be difficult to read.
audits.basis: PASSAGE RETRIEVED. The record lists 'a poem, personal correspondences, personal notes and contacts, divination techniques' — exactly the entry's genre list — and the title 'Kandoolu Kitaaboolu V' with owner/author 'Issa Diante'. It also supports the entry's anti-collapse rule: the record assigns Issa Diante as both owner and author of original material, while the entry warns against treating the item as one coherent treatise. A Cloudflare-style HTTP 202/empty-body response from the EAP archive-file route (https://eap.bl.uk/archive-file/EAP1042-32-5) blocked that alternate route; the catalogue route was used instead.
audits.access_limit: Item images not inspected; archive-file route on eap.bl.uk returned HTTP 202 with an empty body and was not usable.

audits.claim: The BU NEH Ajami project covers Hausa, Fula, Mandinka, and Wolof with selected manuscript images, Latin-script transcriptions, translations, and recorded readings; it is a comparative entry point, not the complete literature of any language.
audits.source_locator: project description, language-coverage and digitization paragraph
audits.source_excerpt: The project has digitized twenty manuscripts in each language and prepared transcriptions into the Latin script as well as translations into English and French.
audits.basis: PASSAGE RETRIEVED; the page names the four languages ('Hausa, Mandinka, Fula, and Wolof') and adds 'we selected over five manuscripts that were the subject of video recorded recitations/readings by local scholars' — directly grounding the entry's rule that a modern recitation is a dated reading event by named readers, not the original author's performance. The finite 'twenty manuscripts in each language' figure supports the entry's caution that the selection is not a complete literature.
audits.access_limit: Web galleries and manuscript images not opened in this pass; only the project-level description was read.

audits.claim: HMML's Malian partners hold family collections in Timbuktu, Djenné, and other locations; Arabic, Fulfulde, Bambara, and other local languages are listed, so 'Timbuktu manuscript' does not itself mean Ajami.
audits.source_locator: profile fields 'Repositories' and 'Languages'; project description paragraph
audits.source_excerpt: More than 30 libraries from Timbuktu, Djenné, and other locations / Arabic, Bambara, Fulfulde, and other local languages
audits.basis: PASSAGE RETRIEVED. The listed languages include Arabic (non-Ajami) alongside Bambara and Fulfulde, which supports the entry's warning to search by library and actual item language. The description ('family library collections used, safeguarded, and kept within learned families for generations'; 'our work of cataloging ... will continue for many years') matches the entry's custody and continuing-cataloguing framing.
audits.access_limit: Individual Reading Room records not inspected; entry states the same limit.

audits.claim: UCT's BC 151 finding aid documents Bleek's access to prisoners and later custodial arrangements [BLL-H, Wilhelm Bleek biography].
audits.source_locator: opening biography of Wilhelm Heinrich Immanuel Bleek
audits.source_excerpt: From 1870 Bleek had access to Bushmen prisoners at the Breakwater Prison. Later some of the Bushmen were released into his custody and lived at his home in Mowbray
audits.basis: PASSAGE RETRIEVED. The same sentence continues 'where their language and folklore was recorded with the assistance of his sister-in-law Lucy Lloyd', grounding the entry's rule that the coercive collection setting must accompany, not erase, the named speakers' testimony. The entry's own note that the finding aid uses terminology not adopted as neutral labels was respected: the record's wording is quoted only inside this audit record.
audits.access_limit: Correspondence-level and notebook-level items listed in the aid were not examined; aid is a description layer, not the notebooks.

unresolved_or_blocked: eap.bl.uk archive-file route for EAP1042/32/5 returned HTTP 202 with an empty body; the searcharchives.bl.uk catalogue route supplied the record instead (AFR-09).

Web search was unavailable during this pass (quota error), so no additional secondary confirmation of the WOM issue metadata beyond the journal's own archive was attempted (AFR-07 relies on the journal record itself).
No verdict is offered on any substantive historical/epic/material interpretation named as contested in the entry §9; checks were limited to source-to-claim correspondence for the locators above.

entry_edit.summary: AFR-02 correction appended 2026-10-17: Raia 2021 spans printed pp. 65–86 in Manuscript Cultures 17; entry's inspected range pp. 65–71 retained as a reading record but must not be read as the article's extent, and variant-group locators reach pp. 72–86.
